sections.title: What are Misc Advanced Techniques?
sections.content: This note bundles two small, self-contained techniques that each solve a narrow but recurring problem shape and don't have enough surface area individually to justify a full note: **Meet in the Middle** (split a large search space in half, brute-force each half separately, then combine) and **Reservoir Sampling** (pick a uniformly random sample from a stream of unknown or unbounded length, using O(1) memory per item). They share nothing algorithmically - they're grouped here purely because both are real, low-frequency techniques worth knowing rather than being worth a dedicated note each.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Meet in the middle: reach for it when brute force is exponential but the input size is roughly double what brute force could normally handle (n around 30-40 instead of 15-20) - the halving trick turns O(2^n) into O(2^(n/2)). Reservoir sampling: reach for it whenever you must pick uniformly at random from a stream/list where you can't see the total length in advance, or don't want to store the whole thing.
signals: n is around 30-40 and brute force over all subsets would be too slow
split the array/set into two halves and combine results
closest subsequence sum / partition into two parts with minimal difference
pick a random element/node from a stream, list, or generator with unknown length
random sampling without knowing the total count in advance

sections.title: Meet in the Middle
sections.content: For problems asking about all 2^n subsets of a set (e.g. 'does some subset sum to exactly X'), brute force is O(2^n x n) - infeasible past n ~ 20-25. Meet in the middle splits the set into two halves of size n/2 each, enumerates all 2^(n/2) subset results for each half separately (still exponential, but of a much smaller exponent), sorts one half's results, then for each result in the other half, binary-searches (or two-pointers) for a matching/complementary value across the two sorted lists. Total cost: O(2^(n/2) x n) to generate plus O(2^(n/2) log(2^(n/2))) to sort and search - which for n=40 turns a hopeless 2^40 brute force into a very manageable ~2^20 x 2 workload.

sections.title: Reservoir Sampling
sections.content: To pick one uniformly random element from a stream of unknown length N, seen one item at a time: keep the i-th item you see as your current answer with probability `1/i` (replacing whatever answer you were holding). By induction, after processing all N items, every item has ended up as the final answer with exactly probability `1/N` - each later replacement dilutes an earlier item's survival probability by exactly the right amount to keep everything uniform. For a reservoir of size k (pick k uniformly random items, not just 1): keep the first k items unconditionally, then for the i-th item (i > k), replace a uniformly random one of the current k reservoir slots with probability `k/i` (and discard it entirely otherwise) - the same dilution argument generalizes directly.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: `allSubsetSums` generates every subset sum of its half by doubling the array each iteration (append `x` to every existing sum) - classic small-scale subset enumeration. `randomNode` never knows the list's length in advance; `Math.floor(Math.random() * i) === 0` fires with probability exactly `1/i`, which is precisely the reservoir-sampling update rule for a reservoir of size 1.

items.name: Meet in the Middle - Subset Sum / Partition
items.description: Split into two halves, enumerate all subset sums of each, then binary-search or two-pointer across the sorted halves to find a matching or closest pair.

items.name: Meet in the Middle - Two-Group Partition
items.description: Split the array into two groups such that both groups' subset averages/sums satisfy some balance condition - same halving idea, with the combine step checking a relationship between two chosen subsets instead of a single target.

items.name: Reservoir Sampling - Single Random Pick
items.description: Pick exactly one uniformly random element from a stream/structure of unknown size in O(n) time, O(1) space.

items.name: Reservoir Sampling - Weighted / Indexed Pick
items.description: Pick a uniformly random *index* satisfying some condition (e.g. equal to a target value) among a set of candidates seen one at a time, rather than a random element outright.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: Meet in the middle: O(2^(n/2) x n) to generate both halves' subset sums, plus O(2^(n/2) log(2^(n/2))) to sort/search - overall O(2^(n/2) x n), far below brute force's O(2^n x n). Reservoir sampling: O(n) to stream through n items once, O(1) work per item.
sections.space: Meet in the middle: O(2^(n/2)) to store one half's subset sums. Reservoir sampling: O(k) for a reservoir of size k (O(1) for the single-pick case) - never O(n), which is the entire point versus 'store everything, then pick randomly'.
sections.explanation: Both techniques exist specifically to trade an intractable time or space bound (O(2^n), or O(n) memory for an unbounded stream) for a tractable one, at the cost of a more involved algorithm - always confirm the naive approach is actually infeasible before reaching for either.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Splitting the set into halves of very unequal size - meet in the middle's speedup depends on both halves being close to n/2; an uneven split doesn't reduce the dominant exponential term.
Forgetting to sort one half's subset sums before searching the other half against it - without sorting, the combine step degrades back to O(2^(n/2) x 2^(n/2)), erasing the speedup entirely.

In reservoir sampling, using `Math.random() < 1/i` style probability checks with off-by-one errors (`1/i` vs `1/(i+1)`, 0-indexed vs 1-indexed counters) - the replacement probability must exactly match the item's 1-indexed position in the stream.

For reservoir sampling of size k, replacing a *fixed* (not randomly chosen) slot in the reservoir on a hit - the slot to evict must itself be chosen uniformly at random among the k current slots, or the sample stops being uniform.

items.title: Linked List Random Node
items.why: The canonical reservoir-sampling problem - pick one uniformly random node without knowing the list's length up front.

items.title: Random Pick Index
items.why: Reservoir sampling restricted to indices matching a target value - same replacement rule, applied to a filtered stream.

items.title: Random Point in Non-overlapping Rectangles
items.why: Weighted random selection (by rectangle area) via prefix sums plus binary search - a different but related 'pick fairly at random' technique worth knowing alongside plain reservoir sampling.

items.title: Closest Subsequence Sum
items.why: The canonical meet-in-the-middle problem - split, enumerate both halves' subset sums, then two-pointer across the sorted halves for the closest-to-target pair.

items.title: Tallest Billboard
items.why: Meet in the middle where the combine step matches on the *difference* between two chosen subsets from each half, not a plain sum - a step harder than the basic template.

items.title: Split Array With Same Average
items.why: Meet in the middle applied to a two-group averaging constraint - requires reformulating 'equal averages' as a subset-sum condition before the halving trick applies.
